sections.html:
Alabama's capital sits on the Alabama River and doubles as the county seat. Its 2020 population was 200,603. State government, Maxwell-Gunter Air Force Base, hospitals and factories keep the local economy steadier than a one-employer town, but sellers still hit familiar snags with inherited houses, rentals and older homes in need of work.

The county held 105,293 housing units in 2020, with 11.5% empty, so vacant houses are ordinary here. Of the occupied homes, 56.3% have owners inside and 43.7% have renters. A lot of sellers are consequently landlords, and their rentals may have back taxes attached.

Outside the capital the county has just two towns, Hope Hull and Pike Road. An owner in an unincorporated place like Pintlala, Snowdoun or Mount Meigs still answers to the same Revenue Commissioner as someone downtown. Most addresses fall in Montgomery Public Schools; Pike Road runs its own district.

sections.h2: Who bills the tax and when
sections.html:
Houses in the city are assessed and billed by the Montgomery County Revenue Commissioner. The due date is October 1, and delinquency follows December 31. Next come probate court in February, a newspaper notice in April and the tax sale in May.

Value notices originate with the county Board of Equalization. Watch for yours in the spring and open it promptly, because your appeal period runs from the date on the notice itself, not from the day you read it.

Your request, with supporting documents, has to reach the county inside 30 days of the date shown on the notice. There is no charge and no required form, and an informal review ahead of the Board of Equalization is available and encouraged.

Appeal detailWhat to know
Deadline30 days counted from the notice date
FeeNone
Where to send itpropertytaxappeals@mc-ala.org
Phone, real property appeals(334) 832-1327
Helpful documentsClosing statements, appraisals, comparable sales and insurance values

File every supporting document along with the appeal, and sign originals. Someone living out of state may file through a representative, who needs no law license but must submit a signed authorization form.

Once the board has ruled, Alabama Code 40-3-25 allows 30 days to go to circuit court. Prior-year taxes have to stay current while the case is pending.

Because the board works from paper, your file does the talking. Closing statements from nearby sales show what buyers really paid. An appraisal from a refinance or purchase offers a professional opinion. Insurance values indicate the cost of rebuilding. Photos and repair estimates explain a gap between your house and a similar one on the next street.

Put your name and the parcel number on each page, sign the originals and keep copies. Asking for the informal review first may resolve things before the board is involved, and trying costs nothing.

Montgomery summers drag on, with about 86 days a year above 90 degrees and heat indexes frequently at 100 or higher. Spring storms may carry big hail, strong wind and tornadoes, and weakened tropical systems can dump heavy rain.

Inspectors therefore begin with the roof, then check drainage and the air conditioner. A big snowstorm comes about once a decade, which makes freeze damage a smaller worry than heat and storms. If your roof or cooling unit is worn out, a cash buyer will take the house with it.

Deeds go to the probate judge for recording. Before one is accepted, the recording privilege tax of $0.50 per $500 of value under Alabama Code 40-22-1 must be paid, and a form giving the actual purchase price must accompany it.

Any unpaid property tax is deducted from the seller's proceeds by the title company.

  • Get a payoff figure from the Revenue Commissioner.
  • Gather the deed, closing statement and any survey.
  • Record the deed with the probate judge once you close.
  • Buyers should have the house assessed in their own name.

When over four in ten occupied homes are rentals, a Montgomery sale frequently includes a tenant. Check the lease for its end date and any showing rules, and let the tenant know what is coming before a stranger arrives.

Landlords are also the owners most likely to have older tax years open. Find out from the Revenue Commissioner if several years are unpaid, since each gets separate advertising and fees after delinquency. If you pay in pieces, start with the oldest year and save every receipt.

A cash buyer can often close with the tenant staying or with the house vacant. State your preference when you request an offer.

sections.h2: A simple timeline for a Montgomery sale
sections.html:
Week one is for facts. Get the payoff, confirm who holds title and decide whether tenants stay. Week two is for offers: compare the net on each, after tax and closing costs, not just the headline price. After you accept, the title company runs its search, orders the payoff in writing and prepares the settlement statement.

Closing day should hold no surprises if you read that statement ahead of time. Check the tax line, the deed details and your proceeds. Afterward the deed is recorded and the buyer assesses the house in their own name.

If you inherited the house, expect one more step. The title company will want proof of who holds title, and it may ask for papers from the estate before it schedules the closing. Start collecting those early, because a missing document is the most common cause of delay and is rarely something the buyer can fix for you.

Keep the final settlement statement and the paid receipt for your records. If a question about the tax ever comes up later, those two pages answer it.

Owing tax does not prevent a sale. The Revenue Commissioner quotes a payoff, the title company settles it out of your proceeds, and the remainder is yours. A payoff holds only for the date it was figured, so the closer may request a fresh one if closing moves. Try to finish before April advertising, and ideally before delinquency in January.

Anyone appealing a value while planning to sell should raise it with the closing attorney first, because the appeal rules demand current prior-year taxes.

Cash Home Buyers purchases Montgomery houses in their present condition, back taxes included, with the title company paying unpaid property tax from proceeds. Because no lender is involved, no appraisal has to be passed and no repair list answered.

Whoever you plan to call, first locate the deed and the latest tax notice and ask the Revenue Commissioner if anything is owed. With an inheritance, add papers showing the current titleholder.

faqs.q: Who sends Montgomery, Alabama property tax bills?
faqs.a: Bills come from the Montgomery County Revenue Commissioner, who also assesses houses inside the city.

faqs.q: When is Montgomery property tax due?
faqs.a: The due date is October 1, and the account is delinquent after December 31.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Montgomery property value?
faqs.a: Thirty days, counted from the date on your notice. Filing costs nothing.

faqs.q: What documents help a Montgomery appeal?
faqs.a: Closing statements, appraisals, comparable sales and insurance values are good examples. File them with the appeal itself.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Montgomery house that has unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Proceeds at closing pay the balance. Ask the Revenue Commissioner for a payoff beforehand.
